prompt:
You are a senior associate at a California criminal defense appellate firm. The managing partner has asked you to prepare a comprehensive memorandum analyzing the California Supreme Court's decision in People v. Delgadillo, 521 P.3d 360 (Cal. 2022). The firm represents several clients who have filed petitions for postconviction relief under Penal Code section 1172.6 (formerly section 1170.95), and their appeals from denials of those petitions are pending before various Courts of Appeal. The partner needs to understand the practical implications of the Delgadillo decision for our clients' pending appeals.

Attached is the full opinion in People v. Delgadillo, 521 P.3d 360 (Cal. 2022).

Prepare a memorandum addressing the following issues:

1. **Wende Procedures and Section 1172.6 Appeals**: Explain why the California Supreme Court concluded that the Wende procedures do not apply to appeals from denials of petitions under section 1172.6. Analyze the constitutional basis for the distinction between first appeals as of right and other appeals, citing the relevant United States Supreme Court authorities discussed in the opinion.

2. **New Appellate Procedures Established**: Describe the new procedures the Supreme Court established under its inherent supervisory powers for Courts of Appeal when appointed counsel determines that an appeal from a denial of a section 1172.6 petition lacks arguable merit. Specify what notice must be provided to defendants and what options defendants have.

3. **Application to Delgadillo's Case**: Analyze the deficiencies in the notice provided to Delgadillo by the Court of Appeal, and explain how the Supreme Court's voluntary independent review affected the outcome.

4. **Practical Implications for Our Clients**: Based on the decision, advise on what appointed counsel should do when they determine a client's section 1172.6 appeal lacks arguable merit, and what rights our clients have in this situation.

The memorandum should be 5-7 pages, use standard legal memorandum format, and cite to the specific portions of the Delgadillo opinion and the authorities it discusses.

paragraphs: This memorandum addresses the procedures that appointed counsel and Courts of Appeal must follow when counsel determines that an appeal from an order denying a petition for postconviction relief under Penal Code section 1172.6 (formerly section 1170.95) lacks arguable merit. Specifically, the memorandum analyzes the California Supreme Court's decision in People v. Delgadillo, 521 P.3d 360 (Cal. 2022), which held that the Wende procedures established in People v. Wende (1979) 25 Cal.3d 436 do not apply to such appeals, and establishes new notice requirements under the Court's inherent supervisory powers.

paragraphs: The California Supreme Court in Delgadillo held that the Wende procedures do not apply to appeals from denials of petitions under section 1172.6 because such appeals do not implicate a constitutional right to counsel. The Court established new procedures under its inherent supervisory powers: when appointed counsel submits notice that such an appeal lacks arguable merit, the Court of Appeal must provide notice to the defendant that (1) counsel was unable to find any arguable issues, (2) the defendant may file a supplemental brief or letter, and (3) if no supplemental brief or letter is timely filed, the court may dismiss the appeal as abandoned. Although the notice provided to Delgadillo was deficient, the Court conducted a voluntary independent review of the record and concluded that Delgadillo was not entitled to relief under section 1172.6.

sections.heading: III. Background
required_content: Facts of Delgadillo's underlying criminal case
Procedural history of the section 1172.6 petition
Procedural history of the appeal to the Court of Appeal
Reference to Senate Bill 1437 and its purpose
paragraphs: Jose De Jesus Delgadillo was convicted of second degree murder under an actual implied malice theory (Penal Code section 187, subdivision (a)) and gross vehicular manslaughter while intoxicated (Penal Code section 191.5, subdivision (a)) following a head-on collision on May 27, 2015, that killed a passenger. Delgadillo's blood-alcohol level was between .13 and .14 percent approximately two and a half hours after the accident. The jury also found true allegations that Delgadillo fled the scene and had two prior DUI convictions. He was sentenced to 15 years to life.

After the judgment was affirmed on appeal, Senate Bill 1437 (Stats. 2018, ch. 1015) went into effect, creating a procedure under former section 1170.95 (now section 1172.6) for persons convicted of felony murder or murder under a natural and probable consequences theory to petition for retroactive relief. The purpose of Senate Bill 1437 was 'to ensure that murder liability is not imposed on a person who is not the actual killer, did not act with the intent to kill, or was not a major participant in the underlying felony who acted with reckless indifference to human life.' Delgadillo filed a petition for resentencing under this new law.

The superior court denied the petition, finding no 'grounds whatsoever for re-sentencing' because 'defendant was the actual and only participant' in the crime. Delgadillo appealed. Appointed counsel found no arguable issues and filed a Wende brief requesting independent review of the record. The Court of Appeal directed counsel to send the record to Delgadillo and sent notice that counsel's inability to find arguable issues could be inferred and that Delgadillo could submit a supplemental brief within 30 days. Delgadillo did not submit any brief or letter, and the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal as abandoned without conducting an independent review, relying on People v. Cole (2020) 52 Cal.App.5th 1023.

sections.heading: IV. Discussion
required_content: Analysis of why Wende procedures do not apply to section 1172.6 appeals
Discussion of constitutional right to counsel on first appeal vs. other appeals
Analysis of the Supreme Court's supervisory powers
Description of the new procedures established
Analysis of deficiencies in the notice to Delgadillo
Analysis of the voluntary independent review
paragraphs:
A. The Wende Procedures Do Not Apply to Section 1172.6 Appeals

The Supreme Court agreed with the Court of Appeal that the Wende procedures are not constitutionally compelled for appeals from denials of petitions under section 1172.6. The Court explained that the Wende procedures are 'relevant when, and only when, a litigant has a previously established constitutional right to counsel.' (Quoting Pennsylvania v. Finley (1987) 481 U.S. 551, 555.) Criminal defendants have a right to effective assistance of counsel on the first appeal granted as a matter of right from a criminal conviction, as established in Evitts v. Lucey (1985) 469 U.S. 387. However, the Court found that Delgadillo's appeal from the denial of his section 1172.6 petition did not implicate this constitutional right. The Court relied on Pennsylvania v. Finley, which held that states need not provide counsel to indigent prisoners seeking postconviction relief, and In re Sade C. (1996) 13 Cal.4th 952, which discussed the scope of the right to counsel in various appellate contexts.

B. New Procedures Under Inherent Supervisory Powers

Although the Wende procedures do not apply, the Supreme Court exercised its inherent supervisory powers to establish procedures for Courts of Appeal when appointed counsel determines that an appeal from a denial of a section 1172.6 petition lacks arguable merit. The Court specified that when counsel submits notice that such an appeal lacks arguable merit, the Court of Appeal should: (1) provide notice to the defendant that counsel was unable to find any arguable issues; (2) inform the defendant that he or she may file a supplemental brief or letter raising any argument the defendant wishes the court to consider; and (3) notify the defendant that if no such supplemental brief or letter is timely filed, the court may dismiss the appeal as abandoned.

C. Deficiencies in Notice to Delgadillo

The Court found that the notice provided to Delgadillo by the Court of Appeal was 'suboptimal' for two reasons. First, the notice indicated that Wende procedures would apply when they did not, potentially misleading Delgadillo about the nature of his appeal. Second, the notice did not inform Delgadillo that his appeal would be dismissed as abandoned if no supplemental brief or letter was filed. Despite these deficiencies, the Court did not remand the case because it conducted its own voluntary independent review.

D. Voluntary Independent Review

The Supreme Court conducted an independent review of the record 'voluntarily in the interest of judicial economy.' Based on this review, the Court determined that Delgadillo was not entitled to relief under section 1172.6. The Court's analysis focused on the trial court's finding that Delgadillo was 'the actual and only participant' in the crime, which distinguished his case from those eligible for relief under Senate Bill 1437. The Court's voluntary review suggests that even when procedural deficiencies occur, the substantive merits of the petition may be dispositive.

sections.heading: V. Practical Implications for Our Clients
required_content: Guidance for appointed counsel on handling section 1172.6 appeals without arguable merit
Explanation of client rights under the new procedures
Recommendations for ensuring proper notice
paragraphs: The Delgadillo decision has several practical implications for our clients' pending appeals from denials of section 1172.6 petitions. First, appointed counsel must recognize that the Wende procedures do not apply to these appeals. When counsel determines that a client's appeal lacks arguable merit, counsel should file a notice with the Court of Appeal stating that no arguable issues were found, rather than a traditional Wende brief requesting independent review.

Second, under the new procedures established by the Supreme Court, Courts of Appeal must provide specific notice to defendants. Our clients should receive notice that: (1) counsel was unable to find any arguable issues; (2) they may file a supplemental brief or letter raising any argument they wish the court to consider; and (3) if no supplemental brief or letter is timely filed, the court may dismiss the appeal as abandoned. This gives defendants an opportunity to present arguments even when appointed counsel finds none.

Third, if our clients receive deficient notice like Delgadillo did, they may have grounds to challenge the dismissal of their appeals. The Supreme Court characterized the notice in Delgadillo's case as 'suboptimal' because it incorrectly referenced Wende procedures and failed to warn of dismissal as abandoned. Our clients should be advised to carefully review any notice they receive from the Court of Appeal and consult with counsel if the notice does not contain all required elements.

Finally, the decision does not eliminate the possibility of relief for our clients. The Supreme Court's voluntary independent review in Delgadillo demonstrates that Courts of Appeal may still review the merits of section 1172.6 petitions even when procedural requirements are not perfectly followed. However, clients should be counseled that the primary avenue for relief remains filing a supplemental brief or letter within the time specified in the Court of Appeal's notice.

sections.heading: VI. Conclusion
required_content: Summary of key holdings
Final recommendations for handling pending appeals
paragraphs: The California Supreme Court's decision in People v. Delgadillo clarifies that the Wende procedures do not apply to appeals from denials of petitions under section 1172.6 because such appeals do not implicate a constitutional right to counsel. The Court established new notice requirements under its inherent supervisory powers, requiring Courts of Appeal to inform defendants of their right to file supplemental briefs and the consequence of dismissal if they fail to do so. For our clients' pending appeals, we should ensure that appointed counsel follows the new procedures and that clients receive proper notice from the Courts of Appeal. Any deficient notice should be identified and, if necessary, challenged to preserve our clients' appellate rights.

S266305 Second Appellate District, Division Four B304441 Los Angeles County Superior Court BA436900 December 19, 2022 Justice Groban authored the opinion of the Court, in which Chief Justice Cantil-Sakauye and Justices Corrigan, Liu, Kruger, Jenkins, and Guerrero concurred. PEOPLE v. DELGADILLO S266305 Opinion of the Court by Groban, J. In People v. Wende (1979) 25 Cal.3d 436 (Wende), we held the Courts of Appeal must conduct a review of the entire record whenever appointed counsel submits a brief on direct appeal which raises no specific issues or describes the appeal as frivolous. (Id. at p. 441.) This procedure is applicable to the first appeal as of right and is compelled by the constitutional right to counsel under the Fourteenth Amendment of the United States Constitution. (Wende, at pp. 439, 441; see Pennsylvania v. Finley (1987) 481 U.S. 551, 554–557 (Finley); In re Sade C. (1996) 13 Cal.4th 952, 983–984 (Sade C.).) In this case, we granted review to determine the procedures appointed counsel and the Courts of Appeal must follow when counsel determines that an appeal from an order denying postconviction relief under recently enacted remedial legislation lacks arguable merit and to decide whether defendants are entitled to notice of these procedures. The Court of Appeal found that it has no duty to independently review an order denying a petition for postconviction relief under Penal Code former section 1170.95, which defendant Jose De Jesus Delgadillo filed here, when appointed counsel submits notice that the appeal lacks arguable 1 PEOPLE v. DELGADILLO Opinion of the Court by Groban, J. merit.1 The Court of Appeal concluded that since Delgadillo’s appeal does not implicate a constitutional right to counsel, the procedures set out in Wende do not apply. (Finley, supra, 481 U.S. at pp. 556–557; Sade C., supra, 13 Cal.4th at p. 978.) We agree with the Court of Appeal as to this issue. We further exercise our inherent supervisory powers to establish the appellate procedures and the requirements for providing notice to a defendant before a Court of Appeal dismisses an appeal from the denial of a petition under section 1172.6. When counsel submits notice that such an appeal lacks arguable merit, the Court of Appeal should provide notice to the defendant that counsel was unable to find any arguable issues; the defendant may file a supplemental brief or letter raising any argument the defendant wishes the court to consider; and if no such supplemental brief or letter is timely filed, the court may dismiss the appeal as abandoned. In this case, although the Court of Appeal did provide notice to Delgadillo, the notice was suboptimal because it indicated that the Wende procedures would apply when they did not, and it did not inform Delgadillo that the appeal would be dismissed as abandoned if no supplemental brief or letter was filed. However, based on our own independent review of the record, which we undertake voluntarily in the interest of judicial economy, we determine that Delgadillo is not entitled to relief under section 1172.6. 1 Assembly Bill No. 200 (Reg. Sess. 2021–2022; Assembly Bill 200) has since renumbered section 1170.95 as section 1172.6. (See Stats. 2022, ch. 58, § 10.) For clarity, we refer simply to section 1172.6 throughout the discussion section. All undesignated statutory references are to the Penal Code. 2 PEOPLE v. DELGADILLO Opinion of the Court by Groban, J. I. BACKGROUND On the afternoon of May 27, 2015, Delgadillo’s Ford Explorer crossed into incoming traffic and collided head on into a Mazda sedan occupied by a driver and passenger in the front two seats.2 The passenger died from injuries sustained in the accident. The driver of the Ford Explorer, later identified as Delgadillo, fled the scene on foot, and a police dog located him hiding in a building nearby. Approximately two and a half hours after the accident, two breath tests showed Delgadillo’s blood- alcohol level to be .13 and .14 percent. Two hours later, Delgadillo provided a blood sample that showed a blood-alcohol level of .13 percent. A jury convicted Delgadillo of second degree murder under an actual implied malice theory (§ 187, subd. (a)) and gross vehicular manslaughter while intoxicated (§ 191.5, subd. (a)). The jury also found true allegations that Delgadillo fled the scene (Veh. Code, § 20001, subd. (c)) and had two prior convictions for driving while under the influence of alcohol (Veh. Code, § 23152). The court sentenced Delgadillo to a term of 15 years to life. The judgment was affirmed on appeal. After the appeal was final, Senate Bill No. 1437 (2017– 2018 Reg. Sess.) (Senate Bill 1437; Stats. 2018, ch. 1015) went into effect and barred a conviction for murder under the natural and probable consequences theory as well as limited the scope of the felony-murder rule. (§ 188, subd. (a)(3), as amended by Stats. 2018, ch. 1015, § 2; § 189; see People v. Gentile (2020) 10 Cal.5th 830, 838.) This change in the law was “to ensure that 2 The brief summary of facts is drawn from the Court of Appeal’s prior opinion in Delgadillo’s direct appeal. 3 PEOPLE v. DELGADILLO Opinion of the Court by Groban, J. murder liability is not imposed on a person who is not the actual killer, did not act with the intent to kill, or was not a major participant in the underlying felony who acted with reckless indifference to human life.” (Sen. Bill 1437, § 1, subd. (f).) Senate Bill 1437 further created a procedure under former section 1170.95 for persons convicted of felony murder or murder under a natural and probable consequences theory to petition for retroactive relief.3 Delgadillo filed a petition for resentencing pursuant to this new law. After the cause was submitted upon written briefing, the superior court denied the petition at a hearing. The superior court found no “grounds whatsoever for re-sentencing” because “defendant was the actual and only participant” in the crime. An order to show cause did not issue. Delgadillo filed an appeal. Appointed counsel found no arguable issues in the appeal and filed a brief in accordance with the procedures outlined in Wende. Sess.) (Senate Bill 775; Stats. 2021, ch. 551). Senate Bill 775 codified and clarified People v. Lewis (2021) 11 Cal.5th 952, 961–972 (Lewis), reaffirmed that beyond a reasonable doubt is the proper burden of proof for a former section 1170.95 resentencing hearing, and expanded former section 1170.95’s provisions to apply also to persons convicted of attempted murder or manslaughter. (Sen. Bill 775, § 1, subds. (a)–(d).) As mentioned above, with the passage of Assembly Bill 200, the Legislature then renumbered former section 1170.95 to section 1172.6 without any further substantive change. (See People v. Strong (2022) 13 Cal.5th 698, 708, fn. 2.) 4 PEOPLE v. DELGADILLO Opinion of the Court by Groban, J. record in accordance with Wende. Counsel further stated she had also advised Delgadillo that “he may personally file a supplemental brief” raising “any points which he chooses to call to the court’s attention” and that she had provided him with the record. The Court of Appeal directed counsel to send the record and a copy of appointed counsel’s brief to Delgadillo. The Court of Appeal sent notice to Delgadillo and counsel that “[c]ounsel appointed to represent appellant on appeal has filed appellant’s opening brief. Counsel’s inability to find any arguable issues may be readily inferred from the failure to raise any. (People v. Wende[, supra,] 25 Cal.3d [at p.] 442.) [¶] Appointed counsel is directed to send the record on this appeal and a copy of appellant’s opening brief to appellant immediately. Within 30 days of the date of this notice, appellant may submit by brief or letter any grounds of appeal contentions, or argument which appellant wishes this court to consider.” Delgadillo did not submit a brief or letter within the requisite time. Following People v. Cole (2020) 52 Cal.App.5th 1023, review granted October 14, 2020, S264278 (Cole), the Court of Appeal found, “[T]he procedures set forth in Wende are not constitutionally compelled if a criminal defendant’s appeal is not his or her initial appeal of right.” (People v. Delgadillo (Nov. 18, 2020, B304441) [nonpub. opn.].) When counsel submits notice that such an appeal lacks arguable merit, the Court of Appeal should provide notice to the defendant that counsel was unable to find any arguable issues; the defendant may file a supplemental brief or letter raising any argument the defendant wishes the court to consider; and if no such supplemental brief or letter is timely filed, the court may dismiss the appeal as abandoned. In this case, although the Court of Appeal did provide notice to Delgadillo, the notice was suboptimal because it indicated that the Wende procedures would apply when they did not, and it did not inform Delgadillo that the appeal would be dismissed as abandoned if no supplemental brief or letter was filed. BACKGROUND On the afternoon of May 27, 2015, Delgadillo’s Ford Explorer crossed into incoming traffic and collided head on into a Mazda sedan occupied by a driver and passenger in the front two seats.2 The passenger died from injuries sustained in the accident. The driver of the Ford Explorer, later identified as Delgadillo, fled the scene on foot, and a police dog located him hiding in a building nearby. Approximately two and a half hours after the accident, two breath tests showed Delgadillo’s blood- alcohol level to be .13 and .14 percent. Two hours later, Delgadillo provided a blood sample that showed a blood-alcohol level of .13 percent. A jury convicted Delgadillo of second degree murder under an actual implied malice theory (§ 187, subd. (a)) and gross vehicular manslaughter while intoxicated (§ 191.5, subd. (a)). The jury also found true allegations that Delgadillo fled the scene (Veh. Code, § 20001, subd. (c)) and had two prior convictions for driving while under the influence of alcohol (Veh. Code, § 23152). The court sentenced Delgadillo to a term of 15 years to life. The judgment was affirmed on appeal. After the appeal was final, Senate Bill No. 1437 (2017– 2018 Reg. Sess.) (Senate Bill 1437; Stats. 2018, ch. 1015) went into effect and barred a conviction for murder under the natural and probable consequences theory as well as limited the scope of the felony-murder rule. Wende Procedures The Attorney General argues that Wende and related cases are designed to protect only the indigent criminal defendant’s constitutional right to counsel on direct appeal from a criminal conviction. We agree that since Delgadillo’s appeal from the denial of his petition does not implicate a constitutional right to counsel, the procedures set out in Wende do not apply. The prophylactic procedures in Wende are “relevant when, and only when, a litigant has a previously established constitutional right to counsel.” (Finley, supra, 481 U.S. at p. 555.)
